summary.text: Letting \(c_0=4,c_1=16,c_2=63\) and \(c_{n+3}=4c_{n+2}-c_n\), the proof studies \(D_n=c_{n+1}^2-c_{n+2}c_n\); its recurrence \(D_{n+3}=4D_{n+1}+D_n\), together with the growth of \(c_n\) and the initial cases, yields \(0<D_n\le c_n\). Thus \(c_{n+2}c_n<c_{n+1}^2\le(c_{n+2}+1)c_n\), which exactly characterizes \(c_{n+2}=\lceil c_{n+1}^2/c_n\rceil-1\), so induction identifies the original sequence with \(c_n\) and gives the claimed linear recurrence (hence generating function).

full_proof.text:
Let \((b_n)_{n\ge 0}\) denote the sequence given by the original definition. Thus
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,
\]
and, for every \(n\ge 0\), \(b_{n+2}\) is the greatest integer satisfying
\[
\frac{b_{n+2}}{b_{n+1}}<\frac{b_{n+1}}{b_n}.
\]
Since the terms occurring as denominators will be positive, this condition is equivalent to
\[
b_{n+2}b_n<b_{n+1}^2.
\]
For positive integers \(N,D\), the greatest integer \(A\) for which \(AD<N\) is
\[
A=\left\lceil\frac ND\right\rceil-1.
\]
Indeed, the assertion that \(A\) is this greatest integer is exactly the pair of inequalities
\[
AD<N\le (A+1)D. \tag{1}
\]
Consequently, the original sequence can equivalently be defined by
\[
b_n=\left\lceil\frac{b_{n-1}^2}{b_{n-2}}\right\rceil-1\qquad(n\ge2). \tag{2}
\]
In integer-division notation this is
\[
b_n=\frac{b_{n-1}^2+b_{n-2}-1}{b_{n-2}}-1,
\]
where the quotient is rounded down. We will prove that this nonlinear recurrence is obeyed by the sequence coming from the conjectured generating function.

Define a sequence \((c_n)_{n\ge0}\) by
\[
c_0=4,\qquad c_1=16,\qquad c_2=63,
\]
and
\[
c_{n+3}=4c_{n+2}-c_n\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{3}
\]
We first establish several elementary growth properties of this sequence. These properties also show that all the subtractions in (3) produce positive integers.

We claim that
\[
c_n<c_{n+1}<c_{n+2}\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{4}
\]
For \(n=0\), this is the direct calculation
\[
4<16<63.
\]
Suppose that \(c_n<c_{n+1}<c_{n+2}\). The first inequality in the next shifted pair is already \(c_{n+1}<c_{n+2}\). For the second, (3) gives
\[
c_{n+3}=4c_{n+2}-c_n.
\]
Because \(c_n<c_{n+2}\) and \(c_{n+2}>0\), we have \(c_n<3c_{n+2}\), and hence
\[
4c_{n+2}-c_n>c_{n+2}.
\]
Thus \(c_{n+2}<c_{n+3}\), completing the induction. In particular, every \(c_n\) is positive.

We will also use the stronger estimate
\[
c_{n+1}\ge 3c_n\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{5}
\]
For \(n=0\) and \(n=1\), this follows from
\[
16\ge3\cdot4,\qquad 63\ge3\cdot16.
\]
For an index of the form \(n+2\), recurrence (3) and (4) give
\[
c_{n+3}=4c_{n+2}-c_n\ge3c_{n+2},
\]
because \(c_n\le c_{n+2}\). This proves (5) for every index.

The main issue is now to show that \(c_n\) is exactly the greatest integer allowed by the original ratio inequality. Introduce the integer
\[
D_n:=c_{n+1}^2-c_{n+2}c_n. \tag{6}
\]
We derive a useful recurrence for \(D_n\). Applying (3) at three consecutive indices gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
c_{n+3}&=4c_{n+2}-c_n,\\
c_{n+4}&=4c_{n+3}-c_{n+1},\\
c_{n+5}&=4c_{n+4}-c_{n+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitution and expansion yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{n+3}
 &=c_{n+4}^2-c_{n+5}c_{n+3}\\
 &=c_{n+4}^2-(4c_{n+4}-c_{n+2})c_{n+3}\\
 &=c_{n+4}(c_{n+4}-4c_{n+3})+c_{n+2}c_{n+3}\\
 &=-c_{n+1}c_{n+4}+c_{n+2}c_{n+3}\\
 &=-c_{n+1}(4c_{n+3}-c_{n+1})+c_{n+2}c_{n+3}\\
 &=c_{n+1}^2+c_{n+3}(c_{n+2}-4c_{n+1}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Using \(c_{n+3}=4c_{n+2}-c_n\) in the last expression, and regrouping, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{n+3}
 &=4\bigl(c_{n+2}^2-c_{n+3}c_{n+1}\bigr)
   +\bigl(c_{n+1}^2-c_{n+2}c_n\bigr)\\
 &=4D_{n+1}+D_n. \tag{7}
\end{aligned}
\]

The first three values are
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_0&=16^2-63\cdot4=256-252=4,\\
D_1&=63^2-248\cdot16=3969-3968=1,\\
D_2&=248^2-976\cdot63=61504-61488=16,
\end{aligned} \tag{8}
\]
where \(c_3=4\cdot63-4=248\) and \(c_4=4\cdot248-16=976\). All three values in (8) are positive. Recurrence (7) therefore proves by induction, advancing a block of three consecutive indices at each step, that
\[
D_n>0\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{9}
\]
By the definition (6), this is precisely
\[
c_{n+2}c_n<c_{n+1}^2. \tag{10}
\]
This is one half of the pair of inequalities (1).

For the other half, we prove the upper estimate
\[
D_n\le c_n\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{11}
\]
The first three cases follow from (8):
\[
D_0=4\le c_0=4,\qquad D_1=1\le c_1=16,\qquad D_2=16\le c_2=63.
\]
To propagate this estimate, we need one consequence of (5). Namely,
\[
2c_n+4c_{n+1}\le4c_{n+2}. \tag{12}
\]
Indeed, (5) gives \(c_{n+2}\ge3c_{n+1}\), so
\[
4c_{n+2}\ge12c_{n+1}.
\]
It also gives \(c_{n+1}\ge3c_n\), and in particular \(8c_{n+1}\ge2c_n\). Hence
\[
12c_{n+1}=4c_{n+1}+8c_{n+1}
 \ge4c_{n+1}+2c_n,
\]
which proves (12).

Now suppose the bounds \(D_n\le c_n\), \(D_{n+1}\le c_{n+1}\), and \(D_{n+2}\le c_{n+2}\) are known. By (7),
\[
D_{n+3}=4D_{n+1}+D_n\le4c_{n+1}+c_n. \tag{13}
\]
On the other hand, (12) implies
\[
4c_{n+1}+c_n\le4c_{n+2}-c_n,
\]
and the right-hand side is \(c_{n+3}\) by (3). Thus (13) gives
\[
D_{n+3}\le c_{n+3}.
\]
Induction on consecutive triples proves (11) for all \(n\).

Rewriting (11) by means of (6), we obtain
\[
c_{n+1}^2-c_{n+2}c_n\le c_n,
\]
or equivalently
\[
c_{n+1}^2\le(c_{n+2}+1)c_n. \tag{14}
\]
Combining (10) and (14), we have, for every \(n\ge0\),
\[
c_{n+2}c_n<c_{n+1}^2\le(c_{n+2}+1)c_n. \tag{15}
\]
Since \(c_n>0\), the ceiling characterization (1), with
\[
A=c_{n+2},\qquad N=c_{n+1}^2,\qquad D=c_n,
\]
shows that
\[
c_{n+2}=\left\lceil\frac{c_{n+1}^2}{c_n}\right\rceil-1. \tag{16}
\]
Equivalently, for every \(m\ge2\),
\[
c_m=\left\lceil\frac{c_{m-1}^2}{c_{m-2}}\right\rceil-1. \tag{17}
\]
Thus the linearly defined sequence \((c_n)\) satisfies exactly the original nonlinear extremal rule.

We can now identify the original sequence \((b_n)\) with \((c_n)\). The initial terms agree:
\[
b_0=c_0=4,\qquad b_1=c_1=16.
\]
Assume inductively that \(b_j=c_j\) for all \(j<m\), where \(m\ge2\). Using (2), the induction hypothesis at \(m-1\) and \(m-2\), and then (17), we find
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_m
 &=\left\lceil\frac{b_{m-1}^2}{b_{m-2}}\right\rceil-1\\
 &=\left\lceil\frac{c_{m-1}^2}{c_{m-2}}\right\rceil-1\\
 &=c_m.
\end{aligned}
\]
Strong induction therefore gives
\[
b_n=c_n\qquad\text{for every }n\ge0. \tag{18}
\]
In particular,
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,\qquad b_2=63,
\]
and, from (3) and (18),
\[
b_n=4b_{n-1}-b_{n-3}\qquad(n\ge3). \tag{19}
\]
This proves the asserted linear recurrence, including all cases: at \(n=0,1,2\) the values are respectively \(4,16,63\), while for \(n\ge3\) formula (19) applies.

Finally, let
\[
B(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}b_nx^n
\]
be the ordinary generating function, regarded as a formal power series. The coefficient of \(x^0\) in
\[
(1-4x+x^3)B(x)
\]
is \(b_0=4\). The coefficient of \(x^1\) is
\[
b_1-4b_0=16-16=0,
\]
and the coefficient of \(x^2\) is
\[
b_2-4b_1=63-64=-1.
\]
For every \(n\ge3\), the coefficient of \(x^n\) is
\[
b_n-4b_{n-1}+b_{n-3},
\]
which is zero by (19). Therefore
\[
(1-4x+x^3)B(x)=4-x^2.
\]
Since \(1-4x+x^3\) has constant term \(1\), it is invertible as a formal power series, and hence
\[
\boxed{B(x)=\frac{4-x^2}{1-4x+x^3}}.
\]
Thus the sequence produced by the original greatest-integer consecutive-ratio rule is exactly the sequence with the conjectured generating function.
